entries.name: English oak
entries.leaves: deciduous, rounded lobes, very short leaf stalks
entries.voxel_shape: broad dome-crowned giant, thick fissured trunk, spreading limbs
entries.notes: The keystone species of the temperate forest: hundreds of insects live on one tree. Pollarded veterans can exceed 1000 years and anchor grey-headed woodpecker and oak longhorn beetles.

entries.name: European beech
entries.leaves: deciduous, oval with wavy edges, glossy copper when young, golden in autumn
entries.voxel_shape: tall straight trunk with smooth grey bark, dense oval crown
entries.notes: Forms closed high forests that shade out almost everything beneath; the floor is carpeted with mast in autumn. Drought and wind exposure limit it to moist, sheltered sites.

entries.name: Sugar maple
entries.leaves: deciduous, five-lobed, flaming orange-red in autumn
entries.flowers: small yellow-green clusters before the leaves (April)
entries.fire: survives moderate fire when mature; thin-barked when young
entries.voxel_shape: oval-crowned tree, grey brown bark, spectacular autumn colour
entries.notes: The source of maple syrup; sap tapped in late winter thaws. Leaf emblem of Canada. Climax species of the northern hardwood forest.

entries.name: Silver birch
entries.leaves: deciduous, small triangular, flickering light green
entries.voxel_shape: slender white papery trunk, airy drooping crown
entries.notes: The great pioneer: colonises clearings, dunes and burnt ground, then steps aside for oak and beech. The whitest trunks read from far away and mark the forest edge.

entries.name: American white oak
entries.leaves: deciduous, rounded lobes, deep green above, pale below
entries.fire: survives; thick corky bark, epicormic regrowth
entries.voxel_shape: broad domed crown, huge furrowed trunk
entries.notes: Valued for barrels: its watertight heartwood is why bourbon tastes right. One of the longest-lived trees of eastern North America.

entries.name: Sweet chestnut
entries.leaves: deciduous, long toothed, glossy dark green
entries.voxel_shape: massive furrowed trunk, broad glossy crown
entries.notes: Old stools reach astonishing girths (records over 4 m across) and may live 1000+ years; the Sicilian Hundred Horse Chestnut is the fattest tree of the Old World. A staple winter food across southern Europe.

entries.name: European ash
entries.leaves: deciduous, pinnate with 9–13 oval leaflets
entries.flowers: small dark clusters before the leaves; wind-pollinated (April)
entries.voxel_shape: tall open crown, smooth grey bark cracking into diamonds with age
entries.notes: The traditional wood of axe handles and hurleys, sprung from its elasticity. Chalara ash dieback (Hymenoscyphus fraxineus) is killing most trees across Europe; resistance is the hope.

entries.name: Scots pine
entries.leaves: evergreen needles in pairs, blue-green
entries.fire: survives light fire when mature; thick plated bark on lower bole
entries.voxel_shape: flat-topped gnarled crown, orange-red upper bark, grey-black fissured base
entries.notes: The only pine native to Britain; ancient Caledonian pinewoods are its last wild stands there. The bare orange upper trunk is a reliable field mark.

entries.name: Common hornbeam
entries.leaves: deciduous, oval with strongly parallel veins, coppery in winter
entries.voxel_shape: muscle-bound fluted grey trunk, dense oval crown
entries.notes: The 'ironwood' of Europe: dense, hard, fine-grained, used where toughness mattered. Fluted trunk and ridged bark make it unmistakable among beech relatives.

entries.name: Common alder
entries.leaves: deciduous, rounded with a notched tip, glutinous when young
entries.fruit: small woody cones that persist through winter
entries.fire: killed by fire; resprouts from base
entries.voxel_shape: conical crown, dark grey bark, waterside habit
entries.notes: The wet-feet tree of stream banks and carr; its roots host nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria. Timber is prized for piles and lock gates because it hardens underwater.

entries.name: Tulip tree
entries.leaves: deciduous, notched tulip-shaped, golden in autumn
entries.flowers: greenish-yellow tulip-shaped with orange throats, high in the canopy (May–June)
entries.fire: survives fire when bark thickens; sprouts from root crown after cutting
entries.voxel_shape: enormous straight bole free of branches for most of its height, pyramidal crown
entries.notes: The tallest broadleaf of eastern North America; exceptionally fast-growing yet strong. Straight, limb-free boles made it the classic canoe and mast tree.

entries.name: Eastern white pine
entries.leaves: evergreen needles in bundles of five, soft and flexible
entries.fire: survives when mature; crown fires kill
entries.voxel_shape: huge straight trunk, layered irregular crown of soft five-needle sprays
entries.notes: The tree Britain's Navy chased into North American forest for masts. Very fast-growing straight grain made it the standard softwood of the 19th century.

entries.name: Eastern hemlock
entries.leaves: evergreen, short flat needles with white under-bands
entries.voxel_shape: dense drooping conical crown, cinnamon-brown fissured bark
entries.notes: The most shade-tolerant tree in North America; survives decades under a closed canopy on 5% of full light. Hemlock woolly adelgid is ravaging the species across its range.

entries.name: Wild sweet cherry
entries.leaves: deciduous, oval, finely toothed, copper-bronze in autumn
entries.flowers: white clusters in spring before or with the leaves (April)
entries.voxel_shape: straight trunk with mahogany-brown bark and horizontal lenticels, broad oval crown
entries.notes: The ancestor of all cultivated cherries. Its red-listed timber is the most prized cabinet wood in Europe; flocks of starlings strip a whole tree in an afternoon.

entries.name: Rowan
entries.leaves: deciduous, pinnate leaflets, grey-green
entries.voxel_shape: small round-crowned tree, smooth grey bark, bright berry clusters
entries.notes: The mountain ash of folklore; planted at doors to ward off witches. Berries ripen just as thrushes fatten up for winter migration.

entries.name: Common hazel
entries.leaves: deciduous, broadly rounded, softly hairy
entries.flowers: yellow catkins (male) and red tufts (female) in late winter (February–March)
entries.voxel_shape: multi-stemmed bush with broad leaves and dangling catkins
entries.notes: Often a coppice rather than a tree: managed on 5–15 year rotations. Hazel with bluebells signals ancient woodland, and hazel dormice depend on nuts every autumn.

entries.name: Common hawthorn
entries.leaves: deciduous, deeply lobed, dark green
entries.flowers: white May blossom, heavy scent, insect-pollinated (May)
entries.voxel_shape: thorny rounded bush or small tree, gnarled with age
entries.notes: The hedge tree of Europe; a single old hawthorn is a dining hall for winter birds. May blossom marks both the old calendar and the fractious start of hay season.

entries.name: Blackthorn
entries.leaves: deciduous, small oval, dark green
entries.fruit: small blue-black sloes with a waxy bloom
entries.voxel_shape: dense spiny thicket spreading by suckers
entries.notes: The hedgehog of shrubs: nothing walks through a mature blackthorn thicket unscratched. Flowers before leaf, so entire bushes flash white in early spring.

entries.name: Elder
entries.leaves: deciduous, pinnate, strongly scented when crushed
entries.flowers: creamy flat umbels in June; insect-pollinated
entries.voxel_shape: broad umbrella-shaped shrub with pith-filled stems
entries.notes: Grows wherever its seeds land, fed by birds; pithy stems snap easily and resprout. Elderflower cordial is the canonical country drink.

entries.name: Common juniper
entries.leaves: evergreen awl-shaped needles in threes, white band below
entries.fruit: fleshy blue-black cones after two years
entries.fire: killed by fire; slow to re-establish
entries.voxel_shape: prickly conical bush, blue-green
entries.notes: The shrub that flavours gin; juniper scrub is open-grown and ancient in old pasture woodland. Juniper decline is a major heathland conservation worry.

entries.name: Dog rose
entries.leaves: deciduous, 5–7 oval leaflets, toothed
entries.flowers: single pale pink to white flowers (June–August)
entries.fruit: red oval rose hips full of seeds
entries.voxel_shape: arching thorny rambler over the canopy edge
entries.notes: Binds the forest edge and hedgerow into a thorned barrier. Hips were the wartime vitamin C staple; leaves host many rose-feeding moths.

entries.name: Bracken
entries.leaves: large triangular divided fronds, dies back in winter
entries.fire: unharmed; spreads after fire via deep rhizomes
entries.voxel_shape: arching triangular fronds forming dense 2 m thickets
entries.notes: Toxic to livestock via ptaquiloside; its rhizome network persists for decades and can dominate cleared ground. Best left alone by the careless and the grazing pony.

entries.name: Wood anemone
entries.leaves: deeply divided into three lobes, dark green
entries.voxel_shape: low carpet of white stars before the canopy closes
entries.notes: Flowers in the brief light before the canopy closes, then vanishes entirely by summer. A classic ancient-woodland indicator; slow-spreading rhizomes carpet old floors.

entries.name: Ramsons (wild garlic)
entries.leaves: broad elliptical, unmistakable garlic smell when crushed
entries.voxel_shape: dense white-flowered drifts along streams
entries.notes: Named for the bears that dig up its bulbs after winter. The whole wood smells of garlic in May; a safe foraging plant that wolves-bane collectors mistake at their peril (the deadly twin is lily of the valley).

entries.name: English bluebell
entries.leaves: glossy dark green, strap-shaped
entries.flowers: nodding violet-blue bells, one-sided on a curved stalk; scented (April–May)
entries.voxel_shape: carpet of nodding blue bells under young beech
entries.notes: Half the world's bluebells grow in Britain; the spectacle peaks with beech in May. Hybridisation with Spanish bluebell is eroding the native stock.

entries.name: Foxglove
entries.leaves: soft grey-green rosettes, downy
entries.flowers: tall spires of purple-pink spotted bells (June–August)
entries.voxel_shape: tall one-spired spikes, scattered along clearings and edges
entries.notes: Biennial that stages its whole bloom in its second summer, then seeds and dies. Beautiful and toxic: every part of the plant is poisonous.

entries.name: Lily of the valley
entries.leaves: broad oval, paired, glossy green
entries.flowers: one-sided sprays of waxy white bells, intensely sweet (May–June)
entries.voxel_shape: low paired leaves with a single spray of white bells
entries.notes: The most scented flower of the forest; favoured by perfumers and lethal to eaters. Whole beds are cloned from one rhizome network.

entries.name: Wood sorrel
entries.leaves: three clover-like heart-shaped leaflets, delicate
entries.flowers: small white bells veined pink or lilac (April–May)
entries.voxel_shape: small clover-like ground carpet tucked in shade
entries.notes: Leaves snap shut at night and open by day; taste is sharply sour from oxalic acid. The forest's built-in lemon peel, small enough to miss.

entries.name: Herb Robert
entries.leaves: very finely divided, crimson-flushed, smells of tom-cat when crushed
entries.voxel_shape: straggly red-stemmed sprawler in shade and wall crevices
entries.notes: Grows where almost nothing else will: between paving stones, on walls, in deepest shade. Bruised leaves smell of phosphorus; old name 'stinking bob'.

entries.name: Wood melick
entries.leaves: bright green, slender, drooping, rough
entries.flowers: open nodding panicles of brown egg-shaped spikelets (May–July)
entries.voxel_shape: low drooping clumps of nodding grass heads
entries.notes: An ancient-woodland marker grass: its nodding brown spikelets hide in dappled shade under beech and ash. Likes the light, base-rich soils of limestone woods.

entries.name: Common ivy
entries.leaves: evergreen, dark lobed juvenile climbing leaves, unlobed adult on flowering shoots
entries.flowers: greenish umbels in autumn — the last nectar before winter (September–November)
entries.fruit: black berries maturing in late winter, bird-dispersed
entries.voxel_shape: evergreen cloak draped over trunks and ground
entries.notes: The forest's winter lifeline: ivy flowers when nothing else does and berries hold through the hungry gap. Strangling-a-tree fear is mostly myth — ivy climbs, it does not kill.

entries.name: European honeysuckle
entries.leaves: deciduous or half-evergreen, paired oval, blue-green below
entries.flowers: cream-yellow to pink trumpets, strongest at dusk (July–September)
entries.voxel_shape: twisting woody climber wound around stems
entries.notes: A dusk-to-dawn perfume custom-built for night-flying hawkmoths. The honeysuckle of A Midsummer Night's Dream draped itself over Shakespeare's hedges.

entries.name: Fly agaric
entries.voxel_shape: red cap flecked with white warts on a white stalk with a skirt and volva
entries.notes: The archetypal fairy-tale toadstool; mycorrhizal partner of birch, pine and spruce. Psychoactive and poisonous in equal measure; the red with white flecks pattern is pure icon.

entries.name: Cep (penny bun / porcini)
entries.voxel_shape: fat brown dome cap on a barrel stem, no gills — spongy tubes below
entries.notes: The king of foraged mushrooms; one good weekend can fetch a kilo before lunch. Mycorrhizal with beech, oak and pine; hunted with obsessive secrecy and no map.

entries.name: Chanterelle
entries.voxel_shape: wavy golden funnel with shallow blunt ridges running down the stem
entries.notes: Apricot-scented and peppery; the false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis) fools beginners with blade-like gills. Slow to crop after rains; a wet week decides the season.

entries.name: Honey fungus
entries.voxel_shape: clusters of honey-brown caps ringing the base of weakening trees
entries.notes: Armillaria mycelia are the largest known organisms on Earth; the Oregon A. ostoyae covers ~9 km² and may be 2500 years old. Foot-long rhizomorph 'shoestrings' girdle host roots.

entries.name: Common haircap moss
entries.leaves: stiff pointed starry leaves with a toothed edge
entries.voxel_shape: springy green star-pile carpets in wet hollows
entries.notes: One of the tallest mosses; its hair-like capsules gave it the name. Beds in bog hollows soak up many times their weight in water.

entries.name: Tree lungwort
entries.voxel_shape: leaflike green-brown lobes plastered onto bark, lettuce-like
entries.notes: A foliose lichen of old, unpolluted woodland; it vanished from most of England with sulphur dioxide and clings to oceanic western refugia. Its cyanobacteria feed the whole canopy.
